speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) whether the Ministry’s plan to only select certain HDB precincts for Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) will result in VERS having a lottery effect; and (b) whether the Ministry can design VERS to apply to all HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: My reply will also address a related question by Mr Andre Low for written answer on 24 September.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Starting from the late 2030s, we will begin to see more HDB flats reach the 70-year mark of their 99-year leases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) and the Housing and Development Board (HDB) will adopt a multi-pronged approach to keep our older flats and estates liveable and vibrant.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, we will upgrade the ageing flats to ensure their safety and liveability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: HIP II will ensure that our older flats are able to last the flat owners till the end of their 99-year lease.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Besides the flats, HDB will also upgrade our older estates and neighbourhoods through programmes such as the Neighbourhood Renewal Programme (NRP) and the Silver Upgrading Programme (SUP).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will ensure that residents who are staying in older estates can continue to enjoy a vibrant neighbourhood with refreshed facilities and greenery.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Complementing these efforts is the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The primary purpose of VERS is to facilitate the orderly redevelopment of ageing estates by spacing out the redevelopment and construction works in towns where there are many older blocks that were built around the same time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I had explained in an earlier media interview, VERS is a complex policy and a long-term undertaking for our society.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will impact existing flat owners and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the policy must be designed carefully to be fair and sustainable for both groups.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We aim to firm up as many of the policy details as possible during this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continually review our processes as we go along and progressively scale up the VERS programme by the late 2030s, when more HDB flats reach their 70-year mark.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, in managing ageing flats and estates, our first priority is to ensure that Singaporeans have a home for life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Today, about 2.5% of HDB households do not own flats that cover the owners to at least age 95.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The current median lifespan of Singaporeans is 84.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Hence, almost all our HDB households own flats with leases that can cover the owners for life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to closely monitor the proportion of HDB households who do not own flats with sufficient duration of leases that can cover the owners to the end of life and keep this number as small as possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, as I mentioned earlier, the primary purpose of VERS is to facilitate the orderly redevelopment of towns where many older flats were built within short periods of time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will allow redevelopment works to be carried out in phases within such towns, which will be less disruptive to residents and heartland businesses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Based on this approach, it is not necessary for every older flat to go through VERS, as we are mindful of the disruption to our residents who will need to relocate when their flats undergo VERS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, VERS, as the "V" suggests, is voluntary.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there could be instances where residents who are offered VERS, collectively decide not to proceed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For residents who do not go through VERS, they can continue to stay in their flats until the leases run out.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will support them in other ways to keep their flats and estates liveable and vibrant, including through upgrading programs like HIP II, SUP and NRP, which I spoke about earlier.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This area of work is an important part of our review as we want to look after residents who go through VERS and also those who do not go through VERS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, HDB flats are sold with 99-year leases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: A leasehold system ensures fairness to future generations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: After 99 years, the land is returned to the state and we can recycle it to build new homes for future generations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This approach allows our current generation to enjoy a diverse range of affordable and accessible housing, while also taking care of the needs of future generations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It improves inter-generational mobility and prevents our society from being split into property owners and those who are not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Low asked how the VERS package would differ from the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) package.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We had explained previously that VERS and SERS have different objectives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SERS is for selected precincts with high redevelopment potential, unlocked through compulsory acquisition.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In contrast, VERS is also to spread out, space out the redevelopment of older towns over time and it will be voluntary in nature.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Based on the questions from Mr Foo and Mr Low, I note that there is broad agreement from both sides of the House that VERS should not create a lottery effect or end up becoming a wealth-generating programme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I agree with these views from both Members.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MND is working out the details of the compensation package.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I thank the Minister for his response.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate it is early days for the VERS policy and I appreciate that we are also in broad agreement about its objectives.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think I just want to raise some supplementary questions to clarify and hope the Minister can clarify that these topics are under consideration as we build up this policy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A lot of them will have paid off their mortgages.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And secondly, I understand the voting process is also being worked out.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps the Minister can also clarify if we are thinking about doing the voting at the estate level or at the block level?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will we deal with situations where let us say three blocks in a five-block cluster have agreed to it, but two blocks are hold-outs?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And also, I understand voting is part and parcel of existing programmes like upgrading.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the consequences of being in the minority that disagrees and is brought along when the majority agrees to the VERS programme, are much heavier for those who are unwilling to participate.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, how will we make sure that the needs of the minority who disagree are met?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Low has also raised some very valid questions in terms of how we are going to carry out the VERS policy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are indeed some of the key considerations that my colleagues and I are currently discussing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I agree with Mr Low that the large majority of the flat owners for the flats that are going through VERS, would likely be seniors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is why we feel that it is important to have that upfront gatekeeping, to ensure that when people buy homes, we keep the number of people who cannot stay in these homes till the end of their lives to be as small as possible, so that homes can be for life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I also agree with Mr Low that the voting process needs to be looked at carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the stakes are higher, as Mr Low pointed out, compared to say, going through HIP.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, certainly I think we would have to pay careful attention to how we manage the voting process to ensure fairness to different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Whether we do it at the estate level or at the block level, I think these are important issues that we need to look at.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not want to jump too far ahead, so I do seek Mr Low's understanding that these are details which I think we would have to share after we have carefully considered the different options.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if you think back on the objectives of VERS, which is to facilitate the orderly redevelopment of older towns where there are many flats that were built around the same period, I think you do need to implement some of this redevelopment, not block by block, but at least a cluster of a few blocks, so that it will be a more orderly process for the redevelopment works.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My view is that indeed we should not create a lottery effect with the implementation of VERS.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also glad that the hon Member, Mr Andre Low, has also agreed that it should not be a wealth-generating tool.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, Mr Low has also raised important points that the Minister has agreed should be considered.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have two further clarifications, I think they elucidate the complexity of the issue.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, the Minister has shared that the intent of VERS is to ensure an orderly redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, because it is going to be voluntary, it is going to be subject to voting.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My question is what levers do we have to ensure that there will be a certain amount of success in the voting process?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If not, then, how does the orderly redevelopment take place.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My second clarification is, to ensure that VERS does not become a lottery, indeed, as the Minister said, to ensure that we have homes for life, it means that the alternatives to ensure that all our Singaporeans have homes that are good and fit for accommodation for the entire duration of the tenures, will need to be important.
So, it is not an enviable task that the Ministry and the Minister has to deal with.
My question is, will we look at VERS together with HIP II and NRP, weigh the considerations in the implementation?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, I think this consideration between how we can help residents who go through VERS and how we can also look after residents who do not go through VERS, is an important one.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I would say that while we are firming up the policy parameters and the details of VERS, it should not stop us from being clear.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because there will be residents who do not go through VERS – either because they are not offered VERS or because they voted not to proceed with VERS collectively – that we will have to make sure that their flats and their estates can remain liveable, can remain safe and can remain vibrant.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the upgrades will also have to pay attention to making the flats senior-friendly and safe.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On top of that, there will be a need to think through the parameters of VERS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because Mr Foo is correct that if we do not have anyone voting for VERS, supporting VERS, going through with VERS, then we cannot achieve the objective of orderly redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is something we will have to think through and strike a careful balance on, so that we are fair to both the existing flat owners, but also to future generations and to keep this sustainable.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am moving on to the next lot of questions.
